text:
Scrap the Parking Mandate

Every city has a rule that most residents have never read and almost everyone pays for. It says that when you build an apartment, a restaurant, a clinic or a corner shop, you must also build a set number of parking spaces. Planners call these minimum parking requirements. They should be repealed, and the sooner the better.

Start with what the rule actually does. A minimum is a government order to build something whether or not the builder, the lender or the customers want it. If parking were as valuable as the rules assume, developers would supply it without being told. The mandate only matters in the cases where the market would build less, which means it forces the creation of spaces that nobody judged worth paying for. Someone pays anyway. The cost is folded into rents, menu prices and the sticker price of everything sold on the lot.

Those costs are not small. A surface space can take up around three hundred square feet once you count the aisles and ramps, and land in a growing city is expensive. A space in a structure or underground can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build. Multiply that by the ratios many codes demand, such as two spaces per unit of housing, and parking can become one of the largest line items in a project. Tenants who own no car still pay for it through their rent. Researchers who have studied this, most famously Donald Shoup, have shown that bundling parking into housing costs forces low-income households, who own fewer cars, to subsidize the cars of their richer neighbors.

The mandate also warps what gets built. Small lots become impossible to develop, because the required spaces will not fit. Historic main streets, with their narrow storefronts and shared walls, could not legally be built today. Old buildings that change use can trigger new parking demands that kill the project. The corner bakery, the fourplex and the small office are exactly the modest, incremental forms that make a neighborhood walkable, and the parking minimum is often the thing that makes them illegal. What takes their place is a low box surrounded by asphalt.

That asphalt has a price beyond money. Land given over to parked cars pays little in property tax compared with the same land holding homes and shops. Cities that carpet their centers with lots end up with thin tax bases, which they then try to stretch across roads and pipes they can barely afford to maintain. The empty spaces also push destinations farther apart, which makes walking and transit worse and driving more necessary. The rule creates the dependence on cars that it claims merely to accommodate.

Defenders raise three objections, and each deserves an answer.

The first is that without minimums, new buildings will flood the street with cars and ruin the neighborhood. But repeal does not ban parking. It lets the people closest to the project decide how much is needed. Developers still want tenants and shoppers, and they know that many will drive. Cities that have removed minimums, including Buffalo, which dropped them citywide in 2017, and Minneapolis, which followed, have seen builders keep providing parking where it makes sense and skip it where it does not. Where street congestion is a real concern, the answer is to price the curb, with permits or meters, rather than to force every building to hide the problem inside its own lot.

The second objection is that the rule protects small businesses and neighbors from spillover. Yet the spillover argument treats public street space as something that must be shielded by private mandates. A better tool is a parking district whose meter revenue pays for local improvements. Residents then gain a stake in having customers arrive, instead of a grievance about every new storefront.

The third objection is fairness to drivers. Plenty of people need cars, and disabled residents need accessible spaces in particular. Nothing here changes that. Accessibility rules are separate from minimum counts and should stay in force. What changes is that drivers pay for what they use, rather than hiding the bill in everyone else's rent.

There is also a plain argument from humility. The numbers in most codes were drawn from manuals that measured peak demand at suburban sites with free parking, then treated those peaks as targets. They were never meant to describe a downtown block with a bus line. No planner can know how many spaces a particular building will need in ten years, when cars, work habits and delivery services will all have changed again. Prices and builders respond to local facts faster than any ordinance can.

Repealing minimums is also one of the cheapest reforms a city can pass. It requires no new spending, no subsidy and no new agency. It simply stops the city from forbidding housing, shops and offices that people would otherwise build. For a country short of homes and worried about affordability and climate, that is a rare free win.

Cities should stop telling builders how much concrete to pour for cars. Remove the mandate, let each project choose, and manage the curb with prices. Parking will not vanish. It will just finally be provided because someone wants it, rather than because a rule says so.
